title: Process Manager: company knowledge that stays alive

elements.label: how to get a cloud project

beats.title: A page everyone uses
beats.notes: Every company has a page that explains how to get something done. How to get a cloud project. How to get a repository.

beats.title: Is it still true?
beats.notes: And every time somebody opens it, they ask the same question. Is this still true?

beats.title: It started to go stale
beats.notes: Usually, nobody knows. The page was right on the day it was written. After that, it slowly went stale.

beats.title: Process Manager
beats.notes: So we built Process Manager. It keeps company knowledge alive, for people and for AI agents.

beats.title: Twice
beats.notes: Stale knowledge costs us twice.

beats.title: A person
beats.notes: A person follows the old page, gets stuck on step three, loses a few days, and finally asks a colleague. Slow, but it corrects itself.

beats.title: An agent
beats.notes: An AI agent reads the same page and simply acts on it. Straight away, and a hundred times a day.

beats.title: Nobody to ask
beats.notes: It never asks a colleague. So the more work we hand over to agents, the more a stale page hurts.

beats.title: Described once
beats.notes: The idea is simple. Every process is described once, in one place.

beats.title: People
beats.notes: People read it in the app, as a map and as a checklist.

beats.title: Agents
beats.notes: Agents read exactly the same description through MCP, the standard way to give an agent access to data.

beats.title: Skills
beats.notes: And when a step can be automated, the description becomes a skill: instructions an agent can run.

beats.title: One answer
beats.notes: So the question, how do I get a cloud project, has one answer. Whoever asks.

elements.text: the first lane is always you

beats.title: Lanes
beats.notes: So what does a description look like? A process is a map with lanes. One lane for everyone who takes part.

beats.title: You first
beats.notes: The first lane is always you. So the first thing you see is your own part of the work.

beats.title: One step, one action
beats.notes: Every step is one action by one person or team. A request. A review. An approval.

beats.title: Decisions and loops
beats.notes: Decisions split the flow, and the way back is drawn too. Rejected? Fix it, and send it again.

beats.title: A result you can check
beats.notes: And it ends with a result you can check. You see the whole journey before you start, including the waiting.

beats.title: The map
beats.notes: In the app, the same description shows up in two ways. First, the map: the whole flow at a glance.

beats.title: Before you start
beats.notes: At the top: what must be in place before you start. An approved cost centre, the right access. If you don't have it, it points you to the process that gets it.

beats.title: The checklist
beats.notes: Second, the checklist. Your steps, numbered, with the exact actions. Which field, which value, which command.

beats.title: Tick as you go
beats.notes: You tick as you go. No more guessing what step three really means.

beats.title: One step, up close
beats.notes: Look closer at one step. It names who does it, what kind of step it is, which tool, and what you get at the end.

beats.title: Kinds of step
beats.notes: There are thirteen kinds of step. A form, a code change, an approval, a wait. Each one tells the reader, or the agent, what sort of work this is.

beats.title: Shared lists
beats.notes: Teams, tools, tiers and languages come from shared lists. Nobody types a team name by hand.

beats.title: Change it once
beats.notes: Rename a team, or change its contact, once. Every process that uses it is right again. One less thing to go stale.

beats.title: For your situation
beats.notes: And a process can say it only applies to tier-zero applications, or only to Go. So you get the answer for your situation, not a generic one.

elements.text:
what people and
agents are given

beats.title: How it stays alive
beats.notes: Now the important part: how it stays alive. First, every process has a life-cycle.

beats.title: Draft
beats.notes: It starts as a draft. Only editors see it, so half-finished knowledge never reaches the people who would trust it.

beats.title: Active
beats.notes: Once it's checked, it becomes active. That's what consumers see, and the only thing agents are given.

beats.title: Retired, not deleted
beats.notes: And when it's retired, it doesn't just vanish. It stays for reference, and points to its replacement. Nobody follows the old way by accident.

elements.text: lists what's overdue, owner by owner

beats.title: An owner and an interval
beats.notes: Second: reviews. Every active process has an owner, and a review interval. Anything from three to twenty-four months.

beats.title: Still correct?
beats.notes: When the time is up, the owner sees a badge and a banner. Is this still correct?

beats.title: One click
beats.notes: If it is: one click, marked as reviewed, and the clock starts again. If it isn't, they fix it first.

beats.title: Reminders send themselves
beats.notes: A small command lists everything that's overdue, grouped by owner. Run it on a schedule, and the reminders send themselves.

beats.title: A date you can trust
beats.notes: So every process carries a date you can trust. And an overdue one is still shown, but with a warning.

beats.title: Who notices first
beats.notes: Third, and my favourite: feedback. The people who notice a stale step first are the ones following it.

beats.title: Flag it
beats.notes: So anyone can flag a step. This doesn't work. One sentence, that's all.

beats.title: Everyone sees it
beats.notes: The step gets a red flag that everyone sees, on the map and in the library. The next reader is warned before they waste their time.

beats.title: The owner fixes it
beats.notes: The owner sees it, corrects the step, and marks it as fixed. The flag goes away.

beats.title: Agents too
beats.notes: Agents can do the same through MCP. So every reader, human or not, is a sensor for stale knowledge.

beats.title: It has to be cheap
beats.notes: All of this only works if writing a process is cheap. Otherwise, nobody does it.

beats.title: Start with what you have
beats.notes: So you start with what you already have. An email, a wiki page, your notes. Paste it in.

beats.title: Any chat assistant
beats.notes: The app builds a prompt, with the rules and the schema. You copy it into whatever chat assistant your company allows. No integration, no API key.

beats.title: The checker
beats.notes: The answer comes back as JSON, and the checker reads it. An unknown team? A step that leads nowhere? A process that never ends? It catches those.

beats.title: Fix, or done
beats.notes: If something's wrong, you get a fix request to send to the same chat. If it's right, you have a map and a checklist. Minutes, not an afternoon.

beats.title: One file per process
beats.notes: Where does it all live? In plain files. One JSON file per process, in a git repository.

beats.title: Every change is a commit
beats.notes: That means every change is a commit. You can see who changed a step, when, and why.

beats.title: Reviewed and checked
beats.notes: Changes can be reviewed like code. And the same checker runs on every push, so a broken process never gets in.

beats.title: Agents can write it
beats.notes: And because they're just files, an AI coding assistant can edit them directly. The repository ships the skills that teach it how.

beats.title: Yours
beats.notes: Nothing is locked inside a tool. It's your knowledge, in your repository.

elements.text: get_my_steps       only what I have to do

it knows how fresh
its knowledge is

beats.title: No second copy
beats.notes: Now the agents. They shouldn't scrape the app, and they shouldn't get their own copy. They read the same files, through an MCP server. The contract is fixed, and the server is the next thing we're building.

beats.title: Search and read
beats.notes: The contract is small. Search for a process. Get the full description.

beats.title: Only my steps
beats.notes: Or ask only for my steps: what I do, with which tool, and what I'm waiting for.

beats.title: Report a problem
beats.notes: And report a problem, exactly like the flag in the app.

beats.title: It knows how fresh
beats.notes: Agents never get drafts. Retired processes point to their replacement. And an overdue review arrives with a warning the agent can pass on. So the agent knows how fresh its knowledge is.

beats.title: Steps without a person
beats.notes: Some steps don't need a person at all. Add a file to a repository. Open a pull request.

beats.title: What and how
beats.notes: A skill is a set of instructions an agent can run to do exactly that. The process says what must happen. The skill does it.

beats.title: Generated when needed
beats.notes: And here's where we're taking it. Process Manager will generate the skill itself, from the description, whenever a step needs one.

beats.title: Self-service
beats.notes: An agent picks it up and does the step in self-service. No ticket. No waiting for another team.

beats.title: A skill that can't go stale
beats.notes: And this is the real point. A hand-written skill goes stale, just like a wiki page. A generated one can't. When the process changes, the skill is generated again.

elements.label:
does your steps:
the form, the pull request

beats.title: Say what you need
beats.notes: Put it all together, and this is where it leads. You say what you need. I need a GCP project.

beats.title: The agent looks it up
beats.notes: Your agent looks the process up, and gets back the steps, the tools and the skills.

beats.title: It does your steps
beats.notes: It does your steps for you. The form. The pull request.

beats.title: You approve
beats.notes: Then it stops, and asks you to approve what it prepared.

beats.title: Approvals stay with people
beats.notes: It never approves anything itself, and it never does another team's part. It waits, tracks, and reports back. Approvals stay with people.

beats.title: Described once
beats.notes: So, that's Process Manager. Every process described once, precisely enough for a machine to act on.

beats.title: Kept alive
beats.notes: Kept alive by a life-cycle, by reviews, and by everyone who uses it.

beats.title: For people and agents
beats.notes: Read the same way by people in the app and by agents over MCP. And turned into skills when a step can run itself.

beats.title: Thanks
beats.notes: Company knowledge that stays alive. Thanks for watching.
